title: What makes a mathematical object forced? A test, three verdicts, and one measurement that failed
abstract: Mathematicians often say that an object had to exist: you cannot subtract in the natural numbers, so the integers appear; you cannot solve x^2 + 1 = 0 in the reals, so the complex numbers appear. The same objects are also called inventions, and both descriptions are usually offered without a test. We propose one, in the form of questions that can be answered yes or no, and we checked the answers in a proof assistant. Question 1: can the old system meet the demand without changing what its elements are? Question 2: among all the ways of extending it, is there a smallest one, determined up to a unique relabelling? Question 3: is the result new, judged against a catalogue of known objects? If Question 2 is answered yes, the object is pinned down: any two smallest extensions are the same up to a relabelling, and the relabelling is unique. We then ran the test on our own work. Three steps of the number tower pass Questions 1 and 2. The step from the rationals to the reals does not: we assert its missing property as a named obligation instead of proving it. A counting invariant proposed inside our programme fails Question 1 outright, because it is already definable on the same carrier. Question 3 is where the test broke: our implementation of 'is it new?' compared the sizes of carriers, and the integers, the rationals and the complex numbers all have the same size, so the test refused everything. We report that failure, since it is the clearest evidence that the test has teeth. What survives is two working questions, one unimplemented third, and a short list of things this approach cannot do.
